name: American Red Cross: disaster relief, home fire safety and services to military families (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: US disaster relief, home fire safety and services to military families.
summary: The American Red Cross responds to home fires and large disasters across the US (shelter, meals, relief items, cash and recovery grants), installs free smoke alarms through its Home Fire Campaign, and relays emergency messages and gives financial help to military families. This model covers that donor-funded work in its fiscal year to June 2025 ($721 million, the domestic disaster, community and armed-forces programmes; the latest audited year, as the FY2026 accounts weren't on the Red Cross's financials page on 4 November 2026) and comes to under 0.003 years of healthy life per $1,000, far below the site's global-health median because almost all the value is money and goods for US households, which the site's one log-income scale values at a small fraction of the same dollar for a household living on a few dollars a day, plus about ten fire deaths averted by smoke alarms. The audited money and goods are measured; the meals and shelter nights (valued by judgment), the smoke alarms and the emotional support, about a fifth of the value before the missing-data step, rest on research on other programmes and on judgment and are discounted for missing data. The biggest uncertainties are what FEMA, insurers and other charities would have provided anyway and how many fire deaths the alarms really avert (the charity's own count of lives saved is nearly thirty times our estimate).

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

People reached with disaster relief and recovery services, FY2025 (Red Cross estimate)

source.title: American Red Cross, Disaster Relief Report: Fiscal Year 2025
source.quote: In fiscal year 2025, we reached an estimated 927,840 people with relief and recovery services, based on number of households reached and average household size.

rows.explainer: The Red Cross's own count, households reached times an average household size: home fires (55,687 in the year) and large disasters. Unique households are not independently verified; the delivery adjustment carries that doubt.

rows.label: Households reached with disaster relief and recovery
rows.explainer: Back to households at the site's US household size, so the people count below uses the same size as every US model.

rows.label: Military families assisted through emergency communication services, FY2025

source.title: American Red Cross, Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2025 (July 2024 - June 2025)
source.page: p. 17, Service to the Armed Forces highlights
source.quote: NEARLY 62,000 families assisted through emergency communication services.

rows.explainer: The armed-forces programme's main service: verifying a family emergency and getting word to the service member's command for emergency leave. Its 1.2 million 'whole health' contacts are brief and not counted as households here.

rows.label: Households served in the year modelled (disaster relief and military families)
rows.explainer: Disaster households plus military families helped with emergency communications. Community Services' partners serve other people, but at these small gains per person the log-income value barely depends on how the value is spread, so it is counted over the same people.

rows.label: People per household
rows.explainer: The site's US household size (persons per consumer unit, @household_size.united_states).

rows.label: People reached
Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: about $740 of full cost per person reached, most of it going to the households with severe losses.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained from emotional and health support per disaster client per year while it lasts (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: The 4% of disaster spending on health and emotional support (disaster mental health, spiritual care, replacing lost medicines and glasses). Its material help is already counted in value delivered below, so this is only the emotional part. No trial measures it: reviews of psychological first aid find no good evidence of an effect on later distress (e.g. Dieltjens et al. 2014, PLoS ONE, a systematic review), so a small best guess with zero as the low end. Anchor: one point-year is roughly the gap between being unemployed and employed; a short conversation after a fire is worth far less.

rows.label: Years the emotional-support effect lasts
rows.explainer: A few weeks to months, as for other one-off support after a loss; no follow-up data.

rows.label: WELLBYs per military family helped with an emergency message
rows.explainer: Getting a service member home quickly for a death or serious illness in the family. Anchor: a close family member's death lowers life satisfaction by roughly half a point to a point for about a year (Clark, Diener, Georgellis and Lucas 2008, Economic Journal, lags and leads of life events); being there rather than not plausibly softens a small part of that (5% of 0.6 point-years is 0.03). Wide, since no study measures it, and the military would verify emergencies another way without the Red Cross (counted in the counterfactual adjustment).

rows.label: WELLBYs per person reached, discounted (emotional support and emergency messages)
rows.formula: (disaster_households * household_size * ls_gain_per_person_year * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, ls_effect_years) + saf_families * saf_wellbys_per_family) / people_reached
rows.explainer: Disaster clients' emotional-support WELLBYs plus military families' emergency-message WELLBYs, spread over everyone reached so the template's bridge row stays as it is.

rows.explainer: Grants to local partners for health, hunger and housing.

rows.label: Share of the assistance that reaches people as money or goods worth what they cost
rows.explainer: Cash and relief items reach people at their cost (1); grants to partner nonprofits (about a fifth of the line) lose the partners' own overhead (about 20%), and donated goods are booked at wholesale prices. So about 0.9 overall.

rows.label: Meals and snacks served, FY2025

source.title: American Red Cross, Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2025 (July 2024 - June 2025)
source.quote: OVER 5.1 million meals and snacks provided with the support of local partners.

rows.explainer: Food in shelters and from mobile kitchens; its cost sits in supplies and contracts, not in the assistance line above.

rows.label: Value of a meal or snack to the person fed (US$)
rows.explainer: What the food would cost the person to buy. Anchor: Feeding America's Map the Meal Gap puts the average US meal cost at about $4 (2023); snacks are cheaper and hot delivered meals dearer. The meals' cost (bought food, and $6.05 million of donated food booked at wholesale, note 1(o)) sits in supplies and contracts, not in the financial and material assistance line, so they are counted once.

rows.label: Overnight shelter and hotel stays, FY2025

source.title: American Red Cross, Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2025 (July 2024 - June 2025)
source.page: p. 6, Disaster response highlights (includes evacuation centres and partners' shelters the Red Cross supported)
source.quote: OVER 274,000 overnight shelter and hotel stays provided.

rows.explainer: Person-nights in congregate shelters and hotels. The 363,000 in the disaster relief report counts only responses costing $10K+ differently; the annual report's figure is used.

rows.label: Value of a night's shelter to the person sheltered (US$)
rows.explainer: What a displaced person would otherwise pay for a safe place to sleep, per person-night: most stays are cots in congregate shelters (worth less than a hotel room), some are hotel rooms shared by a family. Hotel stays the Red Cross pays for may be booked as financial assistance, which is already counted, so the best guess is kept near the value of a congregate night.

rows.label: Money, goods, food and shelter delivered, FY2025 (US$)
rows.formula: (dds_assistance + saf_assistance + cs_assistance) * assistance_value_share + meals_served * value_per_meal + shelter_stays * value_per_stay
rows.explainer: Everything the people reached received, at what it would cost them. The staff time that delivers it (casework, logistics) is cost, not value.

rows.label: Meals and shelter nights' share of the value delivered
rows.explainer: The part of the value that is counted meals and nights at a judged value per unit, not audited money and goods: about a tenth. It weights the branch's missing-data step (the gains are under 2% of a year's consumption, so the log gain splits by value to well under a percent).

rows.label: Value received per person in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: Value delivered spread over everyone reached: a few hundred dollars a person (about $265), much more for the households that lost their homes and less for those who got a meal and a blanket. On the log scale the gains are small enough (under 2% of a year's consumption on average) that spreading them evenly changes the result by under a percent.

rows.label: Average consumption per person in the country (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's US consumption per person, 2024 . FY2025 runs July 2024 to June 2025, so its dollars are about half a year later than the baseline's; US prices rose under 3% in that time, small against the share's range. Changed 2026-11-04 (docs/normalization.md, consumption baselines): the base is the household survey of the people served, the Consumer Expenditure Survey's $32,723 a person in 2024, not the national accounts' $58,517, which also count imputed rents, employer- and government-paid health care and non-profits' spending; the quintile ratios that scale it to the clients are the same survey's. A shared conversion, not thin data.

rows.label: Anchor: consumption per person of the poorest fifth of US households, as a share of the average person's
rows.explainer: The site's shared anchor for a US social service's clients (as in United Way's model): the poorest fifth spend 45% of the average household's (BLS 2024), in households of 1.6 people against 2.4, so per person 0.67 of the average.

rows.label: Home-fire and other local-disaster households: consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: The shared poorest-fifth anchor (0.67 per person) times home-fire households' position relative to it.

rows.label: Large-disaster survivors: consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: The shared poorest-fifth anchor times large-disaster survivors' position relative to it.

rows.label: Home-fire households' consumption per person relative to the poorest fifth's
rows.explainer: Home fires fall most on poorer, renting households, and the campaign and casework target high-risk neighbourhoods: about the poorest fifth (1), from 0.75 (mostly well below the poverty line) to 1.2 (more owners).

rows.label: Large-disaster survivors given help: consumption per person relative to the poorest fifth's
rows.explainer: Those who seek and get disaster financial help skew poor: of FEMA's Individuals and Households Program award recipients in 2002-2024, 64.6% reported household income of $30,000 or less, $0 included, and 85% of $60,000 or less (Congressional Research Service, R48310, Table 7: 'more than half made less than or equal to $30,000'), against a US median household income near $80,000. Consumption is less unequal than income and the Los Angeles fires reached richer neighbourhoods, so a little above the poorest fifth: 1.1, from 0.9 to 1.4 (about 0.74 of the average, 0.6 to 0.94). The incomes are nominal over 2002-2024, so somewhat below today's dollars, which the range allows for.

source.title: Congressional Research Service, FEMA Individual Assistance Grants for Disaster Survivors: Summary of Data and Analysis (R48310, November 2024), Table 7
source.quote: more than half made less than or equal to $30,000

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: Home-fire households and large-disaster survivors at their own shares, weighted by their shares of the money and goods (inc_local_share), so one baseline serves the branch. A year's consumption is the base: the help is counted against a year (income_years), so the short dip right after a loss isn't used.

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person (US$)
Years the value is counted over
rows.explainer: All the help is a one-off sum (cash, goods, meals, nights), counted once at the year's consumption; spreading it over more years would change little at these small gains, and the durable part (furniture, repairs) is in unmodelled benefits.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the clients' own consumption: a dollar does far less for a US household than for one living on a few dollars a day.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: burns averted by smoke alarms (home fires injure about four people per death) and health care in shelters have no outcome data; they are in unmodelled benefits.

rows.label: Homes fitted with free smoke alarms per year (Home Fire Campaign)

source.title: American Red Cross Northern California Coastal Region, press release, January 2025: the 10th anniversary of the Home Fire Campaign
source.quote: Over the past decade, The Red Cross Home Fire Campaign has saved more than 2,000 lives, installed nearly 3 million smoke alarms, made over 1.2 million households safer

rows.explainer: 1.2 million homes over the campaign's first 10.25 years (October 2014 to January 2025) is about 117,000 a year. The FY2025 count isn't published, and the FY2024 annual report gives no running total to difference against the FY2025 one ('more than 3 million alarms'), so the campaign average stands, ranged for a slower or faster year. 'Households made safer' may include visits that gave fire-safety education without fitting an alarm, so the low end is 80,000.

rows.label: Deaths in US residential fires, 2023

source.title: U.S. Fire Administration, Residential fire estimates
source.quote: The 2023 national estimates for residential building fires and losses show that there were: ... 2,890 deaths.

rows.explainer: Civilian deaths in residential building fires, the latest national estimate.

rows.label: US population, 2024
rows.explainer: The site's US population (World Bank), the same figure its US consumption per person divides by.

rows.label: Share of home fire deaths in homes with no working smoke alarm

source.title: Ahrens (NFPA, January 2019), Smoke Alarms in U.S. Home Fires
source.quote: Almost three out of five home fire deaths resulted from fires in properties with no (40%) or no working (17%) smoke alarms.

rows.label: Share of US homes with no working smoke alarm
rows.explainer: About 3-8% of homes have no alarm at all (telephone surveys say 96-97% have one, NIST's correction 92%: NFPA 2019, p. 2), and alarms fail to sound in 12% of fires large enough to trigger them (p. 1), mostly from dead or missing batteries; so roughly 15% of homes have no working alarm. Together with the deaths share above this gives the higher risk of those homes (0.57 / 0.15, about 3.8 times average).

rows.label: Share of the homes the campaign serves that had no working alarm before
rows.explainer: The campaign goes door to door in high-risk neighbourhoods and installs alarms where they are missing or broken; many homes it serves had some working alarm already and get extra ones (a partial gain, counted as none here, which the low end allows for). No published audit of homes' alarm status before installation.

rows.label: Reduction in the risk of dying in a home fire with a working smoke alarm

source.title: Ahrens (NFPA, January 2019), Smoke Alarms in U.S. Home Fires
source.quote: The risk of dying in reported home structure fires is 54% lower in homes with working smoke alarms than in homes with no alarms or none that worked.

rows.explainer: NFPA's national analysis of 2012-2016 home fires: 54% lower; range from the same report's 42% for alarms of any power source present to 63% for hardwired ones. A meta-analysis of the four studies comparing death rates in homes with and without working alarms agrees: the rate is halved (Rohde et al. 2016, Fire Safety Journal, doi:10.1016/j.firesaf.2016.01.008). Both are observational (homes with working alarms differ in other ways), hence the evidence adjustment. The 23% NFPA gives for battery alarms present isn't the low end: it includes alarms with dead or missing batteries, which the campaign's sealed units avoid, and the question here is a working alarm.

rows.label: Years an installed alarm keeps working in the home
rows.explainer: Working alarm-years per home over the alarm's life. Dallas Fire-Rescue's follow-up visits to homes fitted with long-life lithium alarms by its door-to-door programme found 84% working in year 2, 55% in year 4, 27% in year 6, 20% in year 8 and 22% in year 10 (NFPA 2019, p. 6): summed year by year over ten years, about 4.6 working years. The programme's own evaluation agrees: its effect on fire deaths and injuries held for about five years and faded after the sixth (Istre et al. 2014, Injury Prevention, doi:10.1136/injuryprev-2013-040823). Range 3.5 to 6: the Red Cross's sealed units can't have their lithium battery swapped for a shorter-lived one, the failure NFPA names on p. 6, so they may last longer than Dallas's. The first year counts in full, later years discounted.

source.title: Ahrens (NFPA, January 2019), Smoke Alarms in U.S. Home Fires
source.page: p. 6, Dallas Fire-Rescue follow-up of lithium-battery alarms installed 2001-2010
source.quote: In the sixth year group, 71% were present and 27% were working.

rows.label: Home fire deaths averted by a year's smoke-alarm installations (over the alarms' life)
rows.formula: hf_households_per_year * household_size * us_residential_fire_deaths / us_population * hf_served_share_no_working_alarm * hf_deaths_share_no_working_alarm / hf_homes_share_no_working_alarm * hf_risk_reduction * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, hf_alarm_years)
rows.explainer: Homes served × people per home × the national fire death rate × the share that lacked a working alarm × those homes' higher risk × the alarm's reduction × its discounted years. About 10 deaths, against the Red Cross's own count of 295 lives saved in FY2025 (disaster relief report, p. 4), nearly thirty times more: that count is of people who escaped a fire in a home the campaign reached, most of whom would have escaped anyway, and covers alarms installed in earlier years too.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The Home Fire Campaign's deaths averted spread over everyone reached, so the template's bridge row stays as it is. Deaths in the disasters themselves (sheltering before hurricanes) are in unmodelled benefits.

rows.label: Share of the fire deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Children under five die in home fires at about half the general population's rate (USFA) and are about 6% of the population, so about 3% of deaths; the campaign targets families with children (the Red Cross says 775 of its 2,462 'lives saved' were children), so a little more: 4%, from 2.5 to 7%.

source.title: U.S. Fire Administration, Fire risk to children (2019-2023)
source.quote: the relative risk of dying in a fire for the youngest children was 50% lower than that of the general population

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Children 5-9 die in fires at 0.4 and 10-14 at 0.2 times the general rate (USFA, https://www.usfa.fema.gov/statistics/deaths-injuries/children.html), and are about 13% of the population: about 4% of deaths over five (0.13 × 0.3 ≈ 0.04), from 2 to 8%.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Adults 15-49 are nearly half the population at below-average risk; adults 65+ die at 2.5 times the general rate (USFA 2023, https://www.usfa.fema.gov/statistics/deaths-injuries/older-adults.html), so most deaths are over 50, valued by their own ages below.

rows.label: Of the fire deaths averted at 50 or older, share aged 50 to 64
rows.explainer: Population shares over 50 (about 19% of Americans are 50-64, 10% 65-74, 8% 75+) weighted by fire death risk, which rises with age (USFA 2023: 65-74 at 2.2, 75-84 at 2.9 and 85+ at 3.4 times the general rate, https://www.usfa.fema.gov/statistics/deaths-injuries/older-adults.html): about 37% / 31% / 32%.

rows.label: Of the fire deaths averted at 50 or older, share aged 65 to 74
rows.explainer: The same weighting by population and age-rising fire risk: about 31%, from 25% (if the oldest are even more at risk) to 37% (if risk rises less steeply); the rest, about 32%, are 75 or older.

rows.label: Value of a fire death averted at 50 or older (units of value)
rows.formula: hf_share_50_64_of_50plus * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_50_54, @moral_weights.givewell_age_55_59, @moral_weights.givewell_age_60_64) + hf_share_65_74_of_50plus * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_65_69, @moral_weights.givewell_age_70_74) + (1 - hf_share_50_64_of_50plus - hf_share_65_74_of_50plus) * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_75_79, @moral_weights.givewell_age_80_84, @moral_weights.givewell_age_85_plus)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year moral weights mixed by the deaths' ages, as rich-country care requires (families/high-income-care.md), instead of the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band (the over-50s by five-year weights), times your value of a life.

rows.label: Money, goods, food and shelter, in units of value (before adjustments; weights only)
rows.explainer: The income branch's part of uov_bridged, used only to weight the branch adjustments below.

rows.label: Fire deaths averted, in units of value (before adjustments; weights only)
rows.explainer: The smoke-alarm branch's part of uov_bridged, used only to weight the branch adjustments below.

rows.label: Share of the healthy years before adjustments that come through units of value
rows.explainer: The rest are the wellbeing branch's (emotional support, emergency messages).

rows.label: Income's share of the units of value
Money and goods: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Money and goods are counted at their cost, which needs no effect study: the site's cash models take transfers at face value (1). A little below 1 only for the reach behind the spread (households are the Red Cross's estimate, not verified unique households); the judged meal and shelter values are discounted by their own missing-data marker (mc_missing_data_adj), not here.

rows.label: Smoke alarms: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: NFPA's comparison of homes with and without working alarms, and the meta-analysis of such comparisons (Rohde et al. 2016), are observational: homes without them are poorer, with more smokers and older wiring, so the alarm's own effect is smaller than the halving. Against that, installation programmes evaluated against neighbouring homes find effects as large or larger (Dallas, Istre et al. 2014: deaths and injuries combined 63% lower after adjustment, rate ratio 0.32 unadjusted; the Cochrane-style review of controlled trials, DiGuiseppi and Higgins 2000, finds giveaway programmes reduced injuries in two non-randomised trials but no randomised trial measuring deaths). Anchor: observational health effects on the site at 0.5-0.8; 0.7.

rows.label: Emotional support and emergency messages: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: No trial: reviews of psychological first aid find no good evidence of an effect, and the emergency-message value is a judgment from bereavement studies.

rows.label: Share of the money and goods that went to home fires and other local disasters
rows.explainer: Of the 117,000 households given financial assistance, 63,200 were in responses costing $10K+ (disaster relief report, p. 3), so about 46% of households were local disasters, mostly home fires; but they get smaller sums than large-disaster survivors given recovery and bridge assistance. About a quarter of the value.

rows.label: Home fires: share of the help survivors wouldn't have had otherwise
rows.explainer: FEMA gives nothing for a single home fire; renters' and homeowners' insurance covers some (roughly half of US renters have renters' insurance, per insurance industry surveys), family and churches some. The Red Cross is often the only help on the first night: about 0.85, from 0.7 (most insured) to 0.95.

rows.label: Large disasters: share of the help survivors wouldn't have had otherwise
rows.explainer: In declared disasters FEMA's Individual Assistance pays its own awards by its own rules (in North Carolina after Helene, $404.5 million to 157,567 households, about $2,600 each: FEMA fact sheet DR-4827, March 2025), several times the Red Cross's roughly $1,200 per household given financial assistance; insurers, state and local governments and other charities (Salvation Army, church feeding networks, local funds) add more. FEMA's awards follow its own rules and wouldn't be larger without the Red Cross, but others would partly fill the mass-care gap (shelters are often joint with local government). About half, from 0.3 (others fill most of it) to 0.7.

source.title: FEMA, DR-4827-NC disaster fact sheet (Hurricane Helene, North Carolina), 17 March 2025
source.quote: $404.5 million approved for 157,567 households

rows.label: Money and goods: share survivors wouldn't have had otherwise
Smoke alarms: share of alarms the homes wouldn't otherwise have got
rows.explainer: Many fire departments run their own free-alarm programmes, often with the Red Cross; some households would have bought one. The campaign targets homes these miss.

rows.label: Emotional support and emergency messages: share that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: Family, clergy and local mental-health services comfort disaster survivors too, and without the Red Cross the military would verify emergencies through its own chain of command, more slowly.

rows.label: Money and goods: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Measured (1), for the audited part: the financial and material assistance (cash, relief items and grants, the KPMG-audited functional expenses) given to the households the Red Cross counted; money and goods are worth what they cost to the people who get them, which needs no effect study (the site values cash at face value on its one log-income scale), so the outcome rests on the charity's own data. What survivors would have had anyway (the counterfactual) and their consumption are judgments, carried by their own ranged rows. The meals and shelter nights, valued by judgment, take their own marker (mc_missing_data_adj).

rows.label: Meals and shelter: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the meals and nights are the Red Cross's own counts, but their value to the people fed and sheltered ($4 a meal, $40 a night) is a judgment, not a measured cost or price. So the shared missing-data step applies to that part of the money and goods.

rows.label: Smoke alarms: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the homes fitted a year are a campaign average, not the year's count; whether those homes lacked a working alarm is a judgment (no audit of homes' alarm status before installation); and the effect comes from observational studies of other programmes and of homes in general (NFPA 2019; Rohde et al. 2016; Istre et al. 2014), not from an evaluation of the Red Cross campaign. So the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Emotional support and emergency messages: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: both effects are judgments (no trial of the Red Cross's disaster mental-health support or of emergency messages; reviews of psychological first aid find no good evidence of an effect), so the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, a multiplier (the branches' value-weighted average)
rows.explainer: Each branch's evidence adjustment weighted by its share of the value before adjustments: money and goods, fire deaths, wellbeing. Applied through total_adj, it gives exactly what applying each in its own branch would.
rows.formula: uov_share * (inc_share_of_uov * inc_evidence_adj + (1 - inc_share_of_uov) * hf_evidence_adj) + (1 - uov_share) * ls_evidence_adj

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway (the branches' weighted average)
rows.explainer: Each branch's counterfactual, weighted by its share of the evidence-adjusted value, so evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj equals the branches' own products summed: home fires and large disasters for the money and goods, other alarm programmes for the alarms, other comfort for the wellbeing.
rows.formula: (uov_share * (inc_share_of_uov * inc_evidence_adj * inc_counterfactual_adj + (1 - inc_share_of_uov) * hf_evidence_adj * hf_counterfactual_adj) + (1 - uov_share) * ls_evidence_adj * ls_counterfactual_adj) / evidence_adj

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured (the branches' weighted average)
rows.formula: (uov_share * (inc_share_of_uov * inc_evidence_adj * inc_counterfactual_adj * ((1 - mc_value_share) * inc_missing_data_adj + mc_value_share * mc_missing_data_adj) + (1 - inc_share_of_uov) * hf_evidence_adj * hf_counterfactual_adj * hf_missing_data_adj) + (1 - uov_share) * ls_evidence_adj * ls_counterfactual_adj * ls_missing_data_adj) / (evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj)
rows.explainer: Each part's missing-data marker, weighted by its share of the evidence- and counterfactual-adjusted value, so evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × missing_data_adj equals the branches' own products summed: the audited money and goods are measured (1); the meals and shelter (by their share of the value delivered), the smoke alarms and the emotional support are thin (the shared missing-data slider). It moves with the slider only as far as the thin parts' share of the value.

source.title: American Red Cross, Volunteer Connection
source.quote: In the past year, more than 300,000 volunteers contributed over 9 million hours.

rows.explainer: All programmes; about nine in ten Red Cross disaster workers are volunteers.

rows.label: Share of volunteer hours in disaster, armed-forces and community work
rows.explainer: The rest go to blood drives (Biomedical) and training. The Red Cross doesn't publish the split; disaster action teams, shelters and Sound the Alarm events are its biggest volunteer activities.

rows.label: Value of a volunteer hour in the US, 2024 (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's US value of a volunteer hour, 2024 (@united_states.volunteer_hour_value_2024, Independent Sector: the BLS production and non-supervisory wage plus fringe benefits), the local wage the site values volunteers at (Convention 2).

rows.label: Volunteer services already recorded as revenue and expense, FY2025 (US$)

source.title: The American National Red Cross, Consolidated Financial Statements, June 30, 2025 (audited by KPMG)
source.quote: The Organization recorded contributed services revenue and related expense of approximately $47 million and $36 million in 2025 and 2024, respectively. These amounts primarily represent volunteer efforts in support of Disaster Services and Services to the Armed Forces.

rows.explainer: Specialised volunteers (nurses, mental-health workers) whose time the accounts already include in expenses, so in cost: taken off the volunteer value so it isn't counted twice.

rows.label: Partners' own resources behind the same help, as a share of the Red Cross's cost
rows.explainer: Meals are served 'with the support of local partners', many shelters are run with churches, schools and local governments, and fire departments install alarms beside Red Cross volunteers. The partners' own spending isn't published; about 15% of the Red Cross's cost.

rows.label: The Red Cross's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The Red Cross's cost over its cost plus partners' resources plus its volunteers' unpaid time at the US value of a volunteer hour (less the part already booked as expense): about 0.7. Volunteers are a large part of what a disaster response is.
rows.formula: cost_total / (cost_total * (1 + partner_resources_share) + volunteer_hours * volunteer_share_domestic * volunteer_hour_value - contributed_services_recorded)

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: The value delivered is audited spending, so delivery shortfalls are only misdirected or fraudulent claims for financial assistance and relief goods that went unused; the Red Cross has had public criticism of large-disaster logistics (e.g. after Hurricane Sandy), so a little below 1.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Outside effects only (funging inside the Red Cross is in unmodelled benefits): its responses draw in government reimbursement and in-kind gifts (above 1), and its presence may let local governments and other charities do less (below 1, mostly already in the counterfactual). 1, from 0.95 to 1.05.

All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * missing_data_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, the wait and the missing-data step included.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Not modelled: deaths and injuries averted by evacuation shelters before hurricanes and floods (+), burns averted by smoke alarms (+), durable value of repairs and furniture beyond the year (+), preparedness apps and education (+), the 'whole health' and respite programmes for military families (+); against them, money spent in a heavy disaster year on logistics that went unused (-) and funging inside the Red Cross (a gift for a named disaster may let it hold reserves or delay other appeals: about -2%, 0 to -5%). About +8%.
